title: Getting started with mirtverse
text: select_model() fits set candidate models recommends one. dichotomous items compares Rasch, 2PL 3PL models; polytomous items partial credit, generalized partial credit graded response models.  recommended model ordinary mirt object:
code: data <- expand.table(LSAT7) sel <- select_model(data, verbose = FALSE) sel #> mirtverse model selection (ranked by BIC) #>  #>  model npar    logLik      AIC      BIC    SABIC RMSEA   CFI  delta weight #>  Rasch    6 -2664.901 5341.802 5371.248 5352.192 0.040 0.936  0.000      1 #>    2PL   10 -2658.805 5337.610 5386.688 5354.927 0.037 0.968 15.439      0 #>    3PL   15 -2658.055 5346.110 5419.726 5372.085    NA    NA 48.478      0 #>  #> The Rasch model is recommended because it has the lowest BIC (5371.2). The #> runner-up, 2PL, is 15.4 BIC points worse, which is very strong evidence for the #> Rasch model. Likelihood-ratio test Rasch vs. 2PL: chi-square(4) = 12.19, p = #> .016; the 2PL model fits significantly better. Likelihood-ratio test Rasch vs. #> 3PL: chi-square(9) = 13.69, p = .134; the extra parameters of 3PL are not #> needed. Note the tension: the likelihood-ratio test prefers 2PL, while BIC #> penalizes extra parameters and prefers Rasch. Choose Rasch if parsimony matters #> most, or 2PL if fit to these data matters most. AIC would instead select the #> 2PL model. Absolute fit of the Rasch model: RMSEA = 0.040 (close fit), CFI = #> 0.936, SRMSR = 0.047. autoplot(sel) mod <- sel$best

title: Getting started with mirtverse
text: interpret_prompt(mod) packs results prompt can paste AI assistant draft longer narrative. Nothing sent anywhere.
code: interpret(mod) #> Overview #> -------- #> * A Rasch model with 1 dimension was fitted to 1000 respondents and 5 items #>   (EM estimation).  #> * The estimation converged normally.  #>  #> Model fit #> --------- #> * Overall model fit is close: M2 = 23.17, df = 9, RMSEA = 0.040, CFI = 0.936, #>   SRMSR = 0.047.  #> * The chi-square test is significant, but with large samples this is common; #>   the RMSEA indicates the misfit is small in practical terms.  #>  #> Reliability #> ----------- #> * Marginal reliability is 0.42 (low).  #> * Scores are too imprecise for decisions about individuals; consider adding #>   items or using the scores only for group-level summaries.  #>  #> Targeting #> --------- #> * The average item location is -1.33 and the average person score is 0.00, so #>   the test is relatively easy for this group.  #> * Measurement is most precise around theta = -1.36 (information = 1.15, SE = #>   0.93).  #>  #> Items #> ----- #> * Low item-total correlation: Item.5 (r = 0.17). These items relate weakly to #>   the rest of the test.  #> * Misfit: Item.2 (S-X2 p = .002). The model does not describe responses to #>   these items well (alpha = 0.01); inspect them with gg_empirical() or #>   item_card().  #>  #> Local dependence #> ---------------- #> * No item pairs show signs of local dependence (Q3).  #>  #> Person fit #> ---------- #> * 1.4% of respondents have unusual response patterns (Zh < -1.96), which is #>   within what chance alone would produce.

The #>   speed SD is 0.37 on the log-time scale.  #>  #> Items #> ----- #> * The most time-intensive item is Item06 (median 95.0 s); the least is Item17 #>   (median 33.0 s).  #>  #> Rapid responding #> ---------------- #> * 2.9% of responses were flagged as rapid (residual method); 8.0% of #>   examinees have response time effort below .90.  #> * Consider filtering low-effort examinees (motivation filtering) or #>   down-weighting rapid responses before reporting scores.  #>  #> Person fit #> ---------- #> * 8.0% of examinees have aberrant overall timing (l_t p < .05), against 5% #>   expected by chance.

title: Response times and rapid guessing
text: Two rules available. default "residual" rule flags response much faster expected person item. "nt10" rule flags responses faster 10% item’s mean time (Wise & Ma, 2012). what: A Friendly Workflow and Reporting Layer for mirt
title: A Friendly Workflow and Reporting Layer for mirt
text: mirtverse friendly workflow reporting layer mirt package. mirt estimates item response theory (IRT) models; mirtverse helps choose model, understand results, make publication-ready figures, share everything, without writing R code.

title: A Friendly Workflow and Reporting Layer for mirt
text: mirt, developed maintained Dr. R. Philip Chalmers, one comprehensive open-source packages item response theory. introduced Journal Statistical Software (Chalmers, 2012) developed continuously since, version 1.48 released CRAN October 2026. widely used research educational psychological measurement. mirt can: Estimate wide range models: unidimensional multidimensional, exploratory confirmatory, bifactor two-tier, 30 item types (Rasch, 2PL 4PL, graded response, (generalized) partial credit, nominal, ideal-point, nonparametric spline items ), plus user-defined items. Handle complex designs: multiple-group analysis measurement invariance, mixed-effects explanatory IRT (mixedmirt()), latent class diagnostic classification models (mdirt()). Use several estimation engines: EM fixed quasi-Monte Carlo quadrature, Metropolis-Hastings Robbins-Monro (MHRM) algorithm high-dimensional models, several standard-error methods. Check use models: item person fit, limited-information fit (M2), local dependence, DIF differential test functioning, ability estimation (EAP, MAP, ML, WLE, plausible values). mirtverse leaves untouched adds workflow, interpretation reporting tools around .

title: Differential item functioning (DIF) in one call — dif
code: # \donttest{ set.seed(1) a <- matrix(rlnorm(8, 0.2, 0.3)); d <- matrix(rnorm(8)) d2 <- d; d2[1] <- d2[1] - 1 data <- rbind(simdata(a, d, 400, itemtype = "2PL"),               simdata(a, d2, 400, itemtype = "2PL")) gender <- rep(c("F", "M"), each = 400) res <- dif(data, group = gender) res #> DIF analysis: F (reference) vs M; 8 items tested #> Likelihood-ratio tests freeing a1, d; BH-adjusted p < 0.05 flags DIF #>  #>    item     X2 df p.value p.adjusted flag    esd  uesd converged #>  Item_1 47.375  2  < .001     < .001  DIF -0.220 0.220      TRUE #>  Item_2  2.735  2    .255       .529      -0.009 0.059      TRUE #>  Item_3  1.804  2    .406       .529       0.041 0.041      TRUE #>  Item_4  2.441  2    .295       .529       0.037 0.044      TRUE #>  Item_5  1.885  2    .390       .529       0.039 0.040      TRUE #>  Item_6  0.452  2    .798       .798      -0.016 0.016      TRUE #>  Item_7  1.542  2    .463       .529      -0.023 0.043      TRUE #>  Item_8  3.739  2    .154       .529       0.059 0.059      TRUE gg_dif(res)  interpret(res) #> DIF overview #> ------------ #> * Items were tested for DIF between F and M, with F as the reference group (n #>   = 400 F, n = 400 M).  #> * Each item's parameters (a1, d) were freed in turn and compared with a model #>   holding them equal across groups (likelihood-ratio test, BH-adjusted p < #>   0.05).  #> * On the common scale, the M group's mean ability is 0.09 SD below the F #>   group's, and its SD is 1.23.  #>  #> DIF items #> --------- #> * 1 of 8 items show DIF: Item_1 (expected score difference -0.220, favours F; #>   p < .001).  #> * Statistical DIF is not proof of bias: ask content experts whether these #>   items measure something other than the intended ability for one group #>   before removing or revising them.  #>  # }

what: Joint model for responses and response times — fit_rt
title: Joint model for responses and response times — fit_rt
text: Fits van der Linden's (2007) hierarchical framework top fitted mirt model. Response times follow lognormal model, $$\log T_{ij} \sim N(\beta_j - \tau_i, \alpha_j^{-2}),$$ \(\beta_j\) time intensity item j, \(\alpha_j\) time discrimination \(\tau_i\) speed person . Ability speed bivariate normal correlation \(\rho\).

title: Joint model for responses and response times — fit_rt
code: fit_rt(   x,   rt,   flag_method = c("residual", "nt10"),   z_crit = 1.96,   quadpts = c(41, 21),   tol = 1e-04,   maxit = 500,   verbose = FALSE )

title: Joint model for responses and response times — fit_rt
text: x unidimensional model mirt::mirt() fitted item responses. rt matrix data frame response times (seconds, positive unit) rows columns response data. Missing values allowed. flag_method "residual" "nt10"; see Details. z_crit critical value residual method. quadpts number quadrature points per dimension. tol convergence tolerance (largest parameter change). maxit maximum number EM iterations. verbose logical; print log-likelihood estimation.

title: Joint model for responses and response times — fit_rt
text: object class mv_rt elements items (time intensity discrimination SEs), population (speed SD ability-speed correlation), persons (joint ability speed estimates, RTE \(l_t\)), flags (logical matrix rapid responses), logLik, iterations converged. Use tidy(), glance(), augment(), autoplot() interpret() .

title: Joint model for responses and response times — fit_rt
text: item response parameters taken x held fixed; response-time parameters, speed variance ability-speed correlation estimated marginal maximum likelihood EM algorithm two-dimensional quadrature grid. Persons scored jointly, response times act collateral information ability. Standard errors come cross-product individual score contributions. Rapid responses flagged two ways: "residual" marks responses much faster expected person item (standardized log-time residual -z_crit); "nt10" uses normative threshold 10% item's mean time (Wise & Ma, 2012). Response time effort (RTE; Wise & Kong, 2005) proportion person's responses flagged. \(l_t\) person-fit statistic (van der Linden & Guo, 2008) flags aberrant overall timing.

title: Joint model for responses and response times — fit_rt
text: van der Linden, W. J. (2007). hierarchical framework modeling speed accuracy test items. Psychometrika, 72, 287-308. van der Linden, W. J., & Guo, F. (2008). Bayesian procedures identifying aberrant response-time patterns adaptive testing. Psychometrika, 73, 365-384. Wise, S. L., & Kong, X. (2005). Response time effort: new measure examinee motivation computer-based tests. Applied Measurement Education, 18, 163-183. Wise, S. L., & Ma, L. (2012). Setting response time thresholds CAT item pool: normative threshold method. Paper presented NCME.

title: Plain-language interpretation of IRT results — interpret.mv_dif
text: Rules thumb used: RMSEA (M2/C2): <= .05 close, <= .08 reasonable, <= .10 mediocre, otherwise poor. Marginal reliability: >= .90 excellent, >= .80 good, >= .70 acceptable. Discrimination: < 0.5 low, > 4 suspiciously high; location beyond +/- 3 extreme; guessing > .30 high; S-X2 p < alpha misfit. Local dependence: Q3 0.2 average Q3. Person fit: Zh < -1.96 flags aberrant response patterns.

title: Plain-language interpretation of IRT results — interpret.mv_dif
code: mod <- mirt(expand.table(LSAT7), 1, verbose = FALSE) interpret(mod) #> Overview #> -------- #> * A 2PL model with 1 dimension was fitted to 1000 respondents and 5 items (EM #>   estimation).  #> * The estimation converged normally.  #>  #> Model fit #> --------- #> * Overall model fit is close: M2 = 11.94, df = 5, RMSEA = 0.037, CFI = 0.968, #>   SRMSR = 0.032.  #> * The chi-square test is significant, but with large samples this is common; #>   the RMSEA indicates the misfit is small in practical terms.  #>  #> Reliability #> ----------- #> * Marginal reliability is 0.44 (low).  #> * Scores are too imprecise for decisions about individuals; consider adding #>   items or using the scores only for group-level summaries.  #>  #> Targeting #> --------- #> * The average item location is -1.37 and the average person score is 0.00, so #>   the test is relatively easy for this group.  #> * Measurement is most precise around theta = -1.08 (information = 1.47, SE = #>   0.83).  #>  #> Items #> ----- #> * Low item-total correlation: Item.5 (r = 0.17). These items relate weakly to #>   the rest of the test.  #> * Misfit: Item.2 (S-X2 p < .001). The model does not describe responses to #>   these items well (alpha = 0.01); inspect them with gg_empirical() or #>   item_card().  #>  #> Local dependence #> ---------------- #> * No item pairs show signs of local dependence (Q3).  #>  #> Person fit #> ---------- #> * 2.1% of respondents have unusual response patterns (Zh < -1.96), which is #>   within what chance alone would produce.  #>

title: mirtverse 0.1.0
text: First release. launch_workbench(): seven-step Shiny app writes reproducible R code. select_model(): compares candidate IRT models explains recommendation. interpret() interpret_prompt(): plain-language summaries mirt results. tidy(), glance(), augment() item_table() mirt models. ggplot2 graphics: gg_trace(), gg_info(), gg_wright(), gg_itemfit(), gg_q3(), gg_scores(), gg_empirical() autoplot(). item_card() item_cards(): item health cards traffic-light status. mv_report(): self-contained HTML report. fit_rt() sim_rt(): joint modelling responses response times rapid-guessing flags, response time effort l_t person fit.
